groups.label: Foundations & Architecture
groups.description: What Kubernetes is, the control plane, nodes, the API, and the object model everything else builds on.

groups.label: Workloads & Pods
groups.description: Pods — the smallest deployable unit — and the controllers that manage them.

groups.label: Scheduling & Eviction
groups.description: How Pods are placed on Nodes, prioritized, and evicted under pressure.

groups.label: Services & Networking
groups.description: Exposing Pods to each other and the outside world; controlling traffic.

groups.label: Storage
groups.description: Volumes, durable PersistentVolumes, and dynamic provisioning.

groups.label: Configuration & Policy
groups.description: Injecting configuration into Pods and policing resource consumption.

groups.label: Security
groups.description: API access control, workload identity, and Pod hardening.

groups.label: Extending Kubernetes
groups.description: Custom resources, operators, and node-level plugins.

nodes.label: What is Kubernetes
nodes.summary: The front door: why you need an orchestrator, what Kubernetes provides (self-healing, rollouts, service discovery), and what it deliberately is not.

nodes.label: Control Plane & Components
nodes.summary: The anatomy of a cluster: kube-apiserver, etcd, scheduler, and controller-manager on the control plane; kubelet and kube-proxy on every node.

nodes.label: Nodes
nodes.summary: The worker machines that run Pods. Covers registration, heartbeats via Leases, node status/conditions, and graceful shutdown.

nodes.label: Controllers & Reconciliation
nodes.summary: The control-loop pattern at the heart of Kubernetes: controllers watch desired state through the API and drive actual state toward it.

nodes.label: The Kubernetes API
nodes.summary: Everything is an API object behind kube-apiserver: discovery, OpenAPI, API groups and versioning. kubectl is just a client.

nodes.label: Objects, Names & Namespaces
nodes.summary: The object model: spec vs status, names and UIDs, namespaces for scoping, plus annotations, finalizers, and owner references.

nodes.label: Labels & Selectors
nodes.summary: Key/value metadata plus selectors — the universal wiring mechanism Services, controllers, and scheduling constraints all use to pick sets of objects.

nodes.label: Containers & Images
nodes.summary: Container images, pull policies and private registries, the Container Runtime Interface (CRI), RuntimeClass, and lifecycle hooks.

nodes.label: Pods
nodes.summary: The smallest deployable unit: one or more containers sharing network and storage. Almost every other concept exists to create, place, feed, expose, or protect Pods.

nodes.label: Pod Lifecycle & Probes
nodes.summary: Pod phases, container states, restart policy, and liveness/readiness/startup probes — the most-referenced page in the whole knowledge base. Init and sidecar containers extend the startup sequence.

nodes.label: Deployment & ReplicaSet
nodes.summary: The default way to run stateless apps: a Deployment declares desired replicas and drives rolling updates and rollbacks through ReplicaSets.

nodes.label: StatefulSet
nodes.summary: For workloads that track state: stable network identities, ordered rollout, and a PersistentVolumeClaim per Pod.

nodes.label: DaemonSet
nodes.summary: Runs one Pod on every (matching) node — the pattern behind log shippers, node agents, and network plugins.

nodes.label: Job & CronJob
nodes.summary: Run-to-completion workloads: Jobs manage retries, parallelism, and completions; CronJobs run them on a schedule.

nodes.label: Autoscaling (HPA / VPA)
nodes.summary: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling adds replicas based on observed metrics; Vertical Pod Autoscaling resizes requests. Node autoscaling grows the cluster itself.

nodes.label: Disruptions & PDBs
nodes.summary: Voluntary vs involuntary disruptions, and PodDisruptionBudgets that keep enough replicas alive during drains and upgrades.

nodes.label: Workload API & PodGroups
nodes.summary: The newer Workload API groups Pods into PodGroups so schedulers can treat them as one unit — the basis for gang scheduling of batch and ML jobs.

nodes.label: kube-scheduler
nodes.summary: Watches for unbound Pods and picks a node in two phases — filtering then scoring — via the extensible scheduling framework.

nodes.label: Affinity & Node Selection
nodes.summary: nodeSelector, node/pod affinity and anti-affinity, and topology spread constraints — how you tell the scheduler where Pods may or must go.

nodes.label: Taints & Tolerations
nodes.summary: The inverse of affinity: nodes repel Pods unless the Pod tolerates the taint. Also the mechanism behind node-condition-based eviction.

nodes.label: Priority & Preemption
nodes.summary: PriorityClasses rank Pods; when the cluster is full the scheduler may preempt (evict) lower-priority Pods to make room.

nodes.label: Node-pressure Eviction
nodes.summary: The kubelet proactively kills Pods when a node runs low on memory, disk, or PIDs — ordered by usage relative to requests and QoS class.

nodes.label: Dynamic Resource Allocation
nodes.summary: The claim-based successor to device plugins for GPUs and other specialized hardware: ResourceClaims, DeviceClasses, and scheduler-integrated allocation. The single largest page in the docs.

nodes.label: Gang Scheduling
nodes.summary: All-or-nothing placement for PodGroups: either every Pod in the group can be scheduled, or none are — essential for distributed training and batch.

nodes.label: Service
nodes.summary: A stable virtual IP and DNS name in front of an ever-changing set of Pods, selected by labels and backed by EndpointSlices. ClusterIP, NodePort, and LoadBalancer types.

nodes.label: Ingress & Gateway API
nodes.summary: HTTP(S) routing from outside the cluster to Services — Ingress plus the more expressive Gateway API that succeeds it.

nodes.label: Network Policies
nodes.summary: Firewall rules for the flat IP-per-Pod cluster network: select Pods by label and declare allowed ingress/egress. Enforced by the network plugin.

nodes.label: Volumes
nodes.summary: Directories mounted into a Pod's containers — from ephemeral emptyDir and projected volumes to CSI-backed persistent storage.

nodes.label: PersistentVolumes & Claims
nodes.summary: Decouples storage from Pods: cluster-level PersistentVolumes are bound to namespaced PersistentVolumeClaims, with reclaim policies, access modes, and snapshots.

nodes.label: StorageClasses & Provisioning
nodes.summary: Named tiers of storage; a claim referencing a class triggers dynamic provisioning of a matching PersistentVolume.

nodes.label: ConfigMaps
nodes.summary: Non-confidential key/value configuration, consumed as environment variables, command-line args, or mounted files.

nodes.label: Secrets
nodes.summary: Like ConfigMaps but for credentials, tokens, and keys — base64-encoded by default, so encryption at rest and RBAC hygiene matter.

nodes.label: Requests & Limits
nodes.summary: Per-container CPU/memory requests and limits. Requests drive scheduling decisions; limits and the resulting QoS class decide who dies first under pressure.

nodes.label: ResourceQuota & LimitRange
nodes.summary: Namespace-level policy: quotas cap aggregate resource consumption and object counts; LimitRanges set per-Pod defaults and bounds.

nodes.label: API Access Control
nodes.summary: Every request passes authentication, authorization (RBAC), and admission control before it touches etcd — the cluster's security choke point.

nodes.label: Service Accounts
nodes.summary: Identities for workloads: Pods authenticate to the API (and beyond) with projected, auto-rotated service account tokens.

nodes.label: Pod Security Standards
nodes.summary: Privileged, Baseline, and Restricted profiles for Pod specs, enforced per namespace by the built-in Pod Security Admission controller.

nodes.label: Custom Resources & Operators
nodes.summary: CRDs add new API types without touching core; pair one with a custom controller and you have the operator pattern — how most of the ecosystem extends Kubernetes.

nodes.label: Device & Network Plugins
nodes.summary: Node-level extension points: device plugins advertise GPUs and other hardware to the kubelet; CNI network plugins implement the Pod network.
